Okay, here's my main point, and why I think literature and high art, any art that stands up to time, is more than simply entertainment. For students engaged with literary criticism, which has been around since the dawn of universities, they should be taught in the following order:

  1. Read the text on their own, have questions or notes based on the established criticism; they come up with conclusions.
  2. Expand on those conclusions in class through open discussion, guided by said established criticism, not catharsis-driven, which happens from inexperience either from the students or the professor.
  3. Read text again, continue to answer broad questions about the text -- in relation to history, the criticism, and human experience in general -- maybe in the form of guided essay tests.
  4. Repeat until the course is over.
  5. Class ends -- hopefully students had a sustained engagement with difficult reading, writing, speaking, and listening, hopefully all from a professor who knows what they're doing.
  6. Continue to explore criticism on texts -- might not even scratch the surface.
  7. Explore what the author may have written about his own texts, which you might have already been exposed to throughout the process.

What I'm getting from you, and I think I got it, is there's no point to explore literature beyond it's practical potential for entertainment, or that doing that might be damaging to some extent, filling them with egotism, bad intellectual habits etc. Mostly, I disagree, but I acknowledge that opinion; I think there's problems in the university today, but literary criticism isn't one of them. Stories are entertainment, first and foremost, of course; there's an economy and a demand -- like when America was still young; we needed a literature because there was none. But the stories that become timeless -- that's what literature is, and it has much more worth beyond it's potential to be entertaining, especially when centered between people willing to have an open dialogue about the text, without resorting to sessions of catharsis. It might sometimes lead to that, but it's ultimately a healthy process, has been for hundreds, if not thousands, of years.

If you're under the impression literary criticism in the university is all a big therapy session, you might've been lied to. Maybe I've been lied to! I vent to my professors, sure, but they vent to me -- because we're friends. In class, we focus on the text, which acts as a springboard to all the dialogue we have. Sometimes we get away from the characters and the mood of the text, and that's okay! It still all comes from the text, and you can't do that with every piece of entertainment. I've tried. You can't talk about The Walking Dead without tripping over the sloppy writing; whereas something like Breaking Bad can absolutely be talked about very deeply. It just depends; some stuff doesn't go beyond it's initial purpose as entertainment.

About the ego stuff: One of the greater benefits of classic literary criticism, I think, it is to grow and learn to master your ego; yes, there's ego in literary circles, but it's no different from anything else. Everyone has ego issues; the point's being aware of it. I'm totally an egocentric asshole; I know that. If dialogue gets heated, that just means I know I'm alive. I don't know.
